segments.text: Imagine you are a scribe in the 1450s.
All day, you hand copy the king's proclamations and send them out across the kingdom.
It is a reliable, steady job.
Then one morning, you hear that a guy in mines built a new machine.
It prints pages a thousand times faster than you can write them by hand.
You have two choices.
You can pretend the new technology isn't happening,
or you can learn the machine well enough to operate it.
Today, AI is the press in this comparison.
You must run it, or someone else will.
AI left the realm of science fiction years ago to become part of your daily routine.
It operates the apps on your phone and powers the tools your first job will hand you on day one.
Most of what it does today, it will do better tomorrow.
This graphic shows a breakdown of exactly where AI already lives in your daily routine.
First, it recommends media by predicting what you might like next.
You interact with this on Spotify, Netflix, and TikTok.
Second, navigation tools predict traffic and your arrival time on apps like Google Maps and Waze.
Third, face recognition validates your identity,
checking whether a face matches you for phone unlocks and photo tagging.
Fourth, voice assistants turn your speech into words when you talk to Siri, Alexa, or Hey Google.
Finally, chatbots carry on direct conversations with you through programs like ChatGPT, Clod, and Gemini.
Looking at this complete picture shows us something clear.
AI was already part of your day before chatbots arrived.
Because you already use it passively, you can start now.
Learn what AI does well, notice where it struggles, and practice using it for something you care about.
Every single project gives you cumulative experience that you can bring to the next one.
Before personal computers, becoming a designer meant spending years at a drafting table,
learning to draw everything by hand.
Desk tab publishing changed that process.
It put powerful design tools on a teenager's desk,
letting them create brochures and posters while actively developing their abilities.
The tool didn't replace skill.
It simply shortened the distance between wanting to do the work and actually doing it.
AI gives you a similar chance to start making things while you build your skills.
This infographic maps out three specific reasons why you'll thrive in the AI future,
if you begin learning now.
First, this is your time.
Building skills while you are in school provides a safe environment to try new things,
ask questions, and learn from the results.
Second, you'll move faster.
AI helps you try out ideas, get immediate feedback,
and tackle projects you otherwise wouldn't know how to start.
Third, you build good habits early.
Starting now means you practice asking good questions,
checking answers, and making your own independent decisions.
Start now.
Build skills you'll carry into whatever comes next.
New tools consistently change how people work.
The steam engine proved this by replacing human and animal physical labor.
Electricity followed, accelerating factory production and increasing output.
The internet then shifted how we process and distribute information across a global network.
Those past technologies were specialized to specific industries.
AI could do it across almost everything.
In July 2025, the White House released an official national strategy document
called Winning the Race, America's AI Action Plan.
The document outlines exactly what the technology makes possible,
predicting it will simultaneously automate physical manufacturing,
accelerate data processing, and generate new creative mediums all at once.
This is the potential that AI presents.
AI is today's printing press.
Learn to run it.
